newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan government closes corrupt commissary.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan government closes corrupt commissary.

text.p: The Guatemalan government on Monday ordered the army to close a corrupt duty-free commissary, and scores of people flocked to a liquidation sale.

Civilians given their first and only chance to buy luxury items at rock-bottom prices crowded into the store. Bargain-hunters zeroed in on a warehouse load of whisky, wheeling out shopping carts stacked with cases of the imported liquor, which was going for $3 a bottle.
Others picked up everything from expensive tennis shoes and champagne to toilet paper and household cleansers.
"It's great that they've closed it so everyone will eat the same," said Felipe Melgar, who stood in line for three hours waiting his turn to buy "stuff that rich people eat."
So many people showed up that soldiers were letting them in 40 at a time.

President Alvaro Arzu ordered the commissary closed earlier this month and appointed an auditing commission to look into complaints of rampant corruption in the management of the giant military store.

The demise of the commissary, which had been a cherished perk for the once all-powerful Guatemalan military, is one of many changes felt by Guatemala's military since a 36-year civil war ended in December with a peace signing between the government and leftist rebels.
Under the terms of the historic peace accord, the National Guard and the Military Police are being phased out, and the role of the army as an internal police force has ended.
From the mid-1950s until 1986, a series of military governments and strongmen ruled Guatemala and waged a counterinsurgency campaign against a small guerrilla army.
Col. Edgar Noe Palacios, army spokesman, told Reuters the commissary was also closed because the government decided that suppliers enjoyed an unfair advantage.
"It became a centre that benefited private individuals" not connected to the army, Palacios said.
The commissary opened in 1962 to sell military personnel duty-free goods and items hard to get in Guatemala.
Palacios said money made from the blow-out sale would go for severance pay for 200 civilian employees who worked at the store.
